findings.title: No dependency spec, README, or run instructions in the repo
findings.quote:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
findings.claim: The repo is three files (experiments.ipynb, depth-map.ipynb, appendix.pdf) with no requirements.txt / environment.yml, no README, and no stated commands or library versions; depth-map.ipynb additionally imports scipy.spatial and sklearn.neighbors.
findings.concern: The 'complete submission' baseline (dependency specification + README with the exact commands to reproduce each figure) is absent, so the environment must be reconstructed by inspection; impact is small because the dependencies are standard and the notebooks are self-contained.
findings.resolution: Add a requirements.txt (pin numpy/scipy/scikit-learn/matplotlib versions) and a short README stating which notebook produces which figure and how to run it.
findings.paper_ref: Checklist item 5 (paper.pdf): 'Attached Jupyter notebooks allow reviewers to verify the plots without writing any extra code.'
findings.reason: The cited lines 1-2 are the notebook JSON opening, not the quoted imports, so the cited evidence does not prove the claim.

findings.title: Paper states λ~CDF 1−(1−t)^q; code actually samples 1−(1−t)^(1/q)
findings.claim: λ is drawn as 1−exp(−E) with E~Exponential(scale=x) and x equal to the figure's x-axis value q; this yields CDF F(t)=1−(1−t)^(1/q), whereas Appendix A states 'cdf given by F(t)=1−(1−t)^q'. Empirically (out/cdf_check.csv) the sampled CDF at t=0.5 for q=5 is 0.13, matching 1−(1−t)^(1/q)=0.129 and not the paper's 1−(1−t)^q=0.969 (max |emp−paper| = 0.93). The same line recurs at line 337 for the Gaussian experiment.
findings.concern: The written formula is the reciprocal-exponent of what is sampled and even contradicts the paper's own adjacent sentence 'As q increases we can expect a higher corruption rate' (true only for the 1/q form, which the code implements), so the figure axis is mislabeled relative to the stated distribution — a description error, not a computational one; the estimator receives the true λ vector regardless, so no result changes.
findings.resolution: Confirm the intended sampling law: the code and the qualitative statement agree on F(t)=1−(1−t)^(1/q); update the Appendix A formula accordingly (or change the sampling if 1−(1−t)^q was intended).
findings.paper_ref: Appendix A, paper.pdf: 'we sample the corruption rates λ i.i.d. from the distribution with cdf given by F(t) = 1 − (1 − t)^q. As q increases we can expect a higher corruption rate.'
findings.reason: The cited sampling line and copied check script show the empirical CDF follows the reciprocal-exponent law while the paper states F(t)=1-(1-t)^q.

findings.title: Fig. 1 panel (B) threshold uses 1/N (d=1) though the figure is 2-D and (21) uses d/N(t)
findings.claim: The threshold that defines panel (B)'s weights is chosen by balancing t² against 1/N(t), i.e. the univariate (d=1) optimum, but the depth map is 2-D (d=2) and the caption says these weights use 'the value of t from (21)', whose balance term is d/N(t)=2/N(t).
findings.concern: For a 2-D illustration the code selects a slightly different threshold than eq. (21) with d=2 would give; both are valid thresholds and this only shifts which low-corruption samples panel (B) averages, so it does not change the qualitative point of the figure.
findings.resolution: Either use d/N(t) with d=2 to match eq. (21), or clarify in the caption that panel (B) uses the univariate balance t²=1/N(t).
findings.reason: The cited code uses t^2 > 1/N for the second depth-map weights, while the paper caption points to Eq. (21), which uses d/N(t), and the plotted data are two-dimensional.
